result: The manuscript establishes background knowledge that microglia continuously monitor synapses in mature healthy brains, but active synaptic remodeling by microglia is rarely directly observed in this context.
evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 represent established background knowledge cited from the literature and provide appropriate context for the study's motivation. These are well-supported statements about the current state of knowledge in the field.

result: Photodamage focally increased the duration of microglia-neuron contacts and dramatically exacerbated the turnover of dendritic spines and presynaptic boutons. The contact area between microglia and dendrites/axons increased after all types of photodamage, with temporal profiles differing between Spine-PD/Near-Spine-PD and Near-Bouton-PD. Contact duration increased from ~23 min (baseline) to 50-70 min after photodamage.
evaluation: Claims C3-C6 and C27-C36 are well-supported by quantitative data from Figure 1 with appropriate statistical tests (GEE analysis with reported p-values). The temporal dynamics, contact areas, and duration measurements are clearly documented with sufficient sample sizes (n=14-16 mice). The comparison to ischemia data (C36) provides appropriate context.

result: All types of photodamage resulted in higher turnover of spines and axonal boutons compared to baseline (<0.05%). The temporal dynamics of turnover matched those of microglia-neuron contact. Mean turnover was highest after Spine-PD, with balanced spine gain/loss after Spine-PD and Near-Spine-PD, but higher bouton formation than elimination after Near-Bouton-PD.
evaluation: Claims C37-C42 are supported by data in Figure 1 (source data 1 and 2) with appropriate quantification methods. The temporal correlation between turnover and microglia contact (C39) strengthens the causal interpretation. Statistical comparisons are provided for key findings.

result: Spine-head filopodia and bouton filopodia were observed after photodamage but not during baseline. Filopodia occurrence was remarkably higher after Near-Bouton-PD (79.55%) than Spine-PD (11.98%) or Near-Spine-PD (23.61%). All boutons forming filopodia were contacted by microglia for an average of 87±33.7 min.
evaluation: Claims C43-C47 are supported by data in Figure 1 (figure supplements 1-2, Videos 4-6). The quantitative differences in filopodia occurrence rates are substantial and clearly documented. The correlation with microglial contact (C47) is important for mechanistic interpretation. Citation to prior work on filopodia function (C45) is appropriate.

result: New and transient spines/boutons were closest to the photodamage site and more often contacted by microglia compared to stable structures. Microglial contact duration was longer with newly formed and lost spines than stable spines. After Near-Spine-PD, filopodia appeared at stable spines, while after Near-Bouton-PD they originated more often at newly formed boutons.
evaluation: Claims C48-C52 are supported by detailed spatial and temporal analysis in Figure 2. The categorization of spines/boutons by stability and their relationship to photodamage distance and microglial contact is well-documented with appropriate statistical comparisons. This provides important mechanistic insight into selective microglial interactions.

result: Microglia depletion using PLX3397 (reducing microglia to 0.6% after 4 weeks) confirmed that elevated spine turnover after Spine-PD and Near-Spine-PD, and generation of presynaptic filopodia after Near-Bouton-PD, are microglia-dependent processes. PLX3397 treatment did not affect baseline turnover but significantly reduced photodamage-induced spine turnover.
evaluation: Claims C7-C8 and C54-C61 are supported by well-designed depletion experiments in Figure 3 with appropriate controls. The dramatic reduction in microglia (to 0.6%) is verified by immunofluorescence. Statistical analysis (GEE with Tukey post-hoc) shows significant effects specifically on photodamage-induced changes, not baseline. The selective effects on different photodamage types provide mechanistic specificity. Sample sizes (n=6 per group) are adequate based on power analysis.

result: PLX3397 treatment had no effect on filopodia length or stability. Spine-head filopodia formation was independent of microglia.
evaluation: Claims C62-C64 are supported by data in Figure 3 (figure supplement 2 and main panels C4, D4). These negative results are important for distinguishing microglia-dependent from microglia-independent processes. The finding that spine-head filopodia are microglia-independent while bouton filopodia are microglia-dependent (C61) reveals mechanistic specificity.

result: The study used 16 adult (3-4 months old) Cx3cr1Cre/Tomato x GFPM Thy-1 male mice expressing tdTomato in all microglia and EGFP in a subset of cortical pyramidal neurons. Imaging was performed in the retrosplenial cortex (RSC).
evaluation: Claims C23-C26 describe the experimental model and are well-documented. The choice of RSC is justified by citation (C26). The transgenic system is appropriate for dual visualization of microglia and neurons. Sample size of 16 mice is adequate for the study design.

result: The authors conclude that microglia react rapidly to photodamaged synapses in the mature brain and establish prominent contacts to promote spine turnover. They argue their approach of targeting single synaptic sites minimizes injury and standardizes the signal compared to previous single-cell photoablation studies.
evaluation: Claims C65-C66 represent reasonable interpretations of the experimental findings (C3-C8, C27-C61) with appropriate citations to related work. The methodological advance claim (C66) is justified by the more focal nature of the damage compared to whole-cell ablation, though the authors acknowledge this is still an injury model distinct from physiological conditions.

result: The authors speculate that microglia-mediated increases in filopodia formation might provide substrate for new associations and may be mediated by BDNF released by microglia in response to ATP. They suggest neurotransmitter release after spine cutting may explain stronger microglial attraction in Spine-PD, and that variability in Near-Bouton-PD/Near-Spine-PD could result from damage to astrocytes or unlabeled neurons.
evaluation: Claims C68-C70, C73-C74 are explicitly speculative (using 'might', 'may', 'could', 'it is possible'). While these hypotheses are reasonable and supported by citations to relevant mechanisms, they are not directly tested in this study. The BDNF/ATP hypothesis (C69-C70) is plausible but requires experimental validation. The explanations for variability (C73-C74) are reasonable but remain speculative.

result: After Spine-PD there was higher microglia attraction toward the targeted spine compared to Near-Spine-PD and Near-Bouton-PD. Higher variability in responses was observed after Near-Spine-PD and Near-Bouton-PD, particularly Near-Bouton-PD.
evaluation: Claims C71-C72 are supported by the quantitative data showing differential contact areas and temporal profiles across photodamage types (C27-C31, C88-C90). The observation of higher variability is evident in the data presentation, though formal statistical tests for variance differences are not explicitly reported.

result: The authors note their observation of microglia-mediated spine remodeling aligns with recent data on microglial elimination of synaptic components in adult hippocampus and findings that depleting microglia or inhibiting microglial phagocytosis prevented forgetting of remote memories.
evaluation: Claims C75-C76 appropriately contextualize the current findings within recent literature (Wang et al., 2020). The comparison is reasonable given the similar involvement of microglia in synaptic remodeling, though the authors acknowledge differences between injury-induced and homeostatic mechanisms.

result: The authors anticipate their methodology will be instrumental in elucidating aspects of synaptic surveillance by microglia and mechanisms of microglia-dependent/independent synaptic remodeling, potentially helping dissect microglial contributions to memory formation under normal and neurodegenerative conditions.
evaluation: Claims C77-C79 are explicitly speculative statements about future applications (using 'anticipate', 'may'). While the methodology does provide a new tool for studying microglia-synapse interactions, the actual utility for understanding homeostatic surveillance and memory processes remains to be demonstrated. The authors acknowledge the difference between injury and homeostatic mechanisms.

result: The study used male mice based on literature showing male microglia have higher motility capacity and are more prone to inflammatory activation than female microglia.
evaluation: Claims C80-C81 are supported by appropriate citations (Lenz and McCarthy, 2015; Villa et al., 2018) and provide reasonable justification for the choice to use only male mice in this initial study. However, this limits generalizability to both sexes.

result: The manuscript provides extensive background on microglial biology, including their roles in immune defense, synaptic elimination during development and injury, interactions with synapses in mature brains, and contributions to various forms of plasticity. Technical background on laser ablation methods and PLX3397 mechanism is also provided.
evaluation: Claims C9-C22, C53, C67, C82-C84 represent background knowledge appropriately supported by citations to relevant literature. These provide necessary context for the study but are not novel findings. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made.
